blocks.text: Intel was founded July 18, 1968, by semiconductor pioneers Gordon Moore (of Moore’s law fame) and Robert Noyce and investor Arthur Rock. Intel’s employee #3 was Andrew Grove. Moore, Noyce, and Grove had all worked together at Fairchild Semiconductor in the mid 1960s.

The name “Intel” means INTegrated ELectronics. Moore and Noyce didn’t want to name the company after themselves, as it would sound like “more noise.” With noise being an undesired property in electronics, they initially chose the name NM Electronics, using their initials, but changed the name to Intel less than two weeks after its founding. Intel was already a trademark of a hotel chain, so the young company bought the rights to the name.
Intel’s IPO
Intel held its IPO on October 13, 1971, raising $6.8 million, or $23.50 per share. It was the very first company on the NASDAQ, a stock market known mostly for technology firms.

Intel played a large role in the rise of Silicon Valley as a high-tech center. Initially Intel was an early developer of SRAM and DRAM memory chips, and that represented the majority of its business until 1981. Although the company created the world’s first commercial microprocessor chip–the Intel 4004–in 1971, it was not until the widespread success of the PC in the early 1990s that CPUs became its primary business. Intel produced CPUs somewhat reluctantly at first, getting into them primarily out of a hope that inexpensive CPUs would help them sell more memory chips.
The transformation into a CPU company

By 1974 Intel had developed the 8-bit 8008 and quickly thereafter, in 1975, the 8080 processor. The 8080 became the core of the Altair, the product that launched the microcomputer revolution. Soon after came the 8086 16-bit microprocessor and a cost-reduced version, the 8088, which IBM chose for its IBM PC. In 1985, Intel produced the 32-bit 80386 microprocessor which began a long line of increasingly powerful microprocessors including the 80486, the Pentium, and a wide variety of supporting integrated circuits and computers built with them. The PC’s popularity turned x86 into a de facto standard.

With the 386 generation, Intel made the decision to stop second-sourcing its CPUs, becoming a sole source instead. This corresponded with then-CEO Gordon Moore deciding to shift focus to CPUs from memory devices in the face of stiff competition from Japanese RAM manufacturers.

With the inability to second-source the designs, other companies started to clone them. Intel litigated most of these early companies, such as Chips & Technologies and UMC, out of the market. Keeping upstarts out during the 486 and Pentium generation proved more difficult, but eventually the Pentium maker was able to use patents to eliminate essentially all but AMD. Yes, Zhaoxin exists selling chips in the Chinese market, but that’s largely for political reasons, not technical.
Intel Inside

The other hallmark of Intel’s glory days was its marketing. It positioned itself as a premium brand, telling you to look for their sticker, and sowing doubt on other chipmakers. It was effective. I worked places who for years wouldn’t even consider an AMD processor, never mind that in the days before CPUs, the conventional processor designs in enterprise-grade minicomputers like the DEC PDP-11 and VAX were full of discrete logic chips made by AMD and AMD 2900-series ALUs. And AMD was a reliable second source for IBM throughout the 1980s, not just for CPUs, but for virtually every other chip on the motherboard.

But AMD couldn’t afford to advertise, so they fell to off-brand status even though there was absolutely nothing wrong with the compatibility or reliability of their chips. Even the notorious Pentium FDIV bug did little to tarnish Intel’s reputation as the premium brand in the 1990s.

Today there’s less perception that there’s something wrong with buying AMD chips, largely because AMD executed with the Athlon 64 generation, then executed again on the Ryzen generation, keeping pace with Intel on performance and power consumption and sometimes exceeding them, because Intel’s lead in chip fabrication processes has eroded over time. There are still people who regard them as a premium brand and buy Intel out of habit. But the days of seeing Intel as the only choice seem to be waning, and it’s reflected in the company’s share price.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

translations: Intel 成立于 1968 年 7 月 18 日，由半导体先驱 Gordon Moore（以摩尔定律闻名）和 Robert Noyce 以及投资人 Arthur Rock 共同创立。Intel 的第三号员工是 Andrew Grove。Moore、Noyce 和 Grove 在 20 世纪 60 年代中期都曾在 Fairchild Semiconductor 共事。

“Intel”这个名字代表 INTegrated ELectronics（集成电子学）。Moore 和 Noyce 不想以自己的名字命名公司，因为这听起来像“more noise”（更多噪音）。由于噪音在电子学中是不受欢迎的特性，他们最初选择使用各自首字母的 NM Electronics 作为公司名，但在成立不到两周后就改名为 Intel。Intel 当时已经是一家连锁酒店的商标，因此这家年轻的公司买下了该名称的使用权。
Intel 的 IPO
Intel 于 1971 年 10 月 13 日进行 IPO，筹集了 680 万美元，每股 23.50 美元。它是 NASDAQ（一家以科技公司闻名的股票市场）上的第一家上市公司。

Intel 在硅谷崛起为高科技中心的过程中发挥了重要作用。最初，Intel 是 SRAM 和 DRAM 内存芯片的早期开发者，直到 1981 年，这部分业务一直占其业务的绝大部分。尽管该公司在 1971 年创造了世界上第一款商用微处理器芯片——Intel 4004，但直到 20 世纪 90 年代初 PC 取得广泛成功后，CPU 才成为其主要业务。Intel 最初生产 CPU 时有些勉强，涉足该领域主要是希望廉价的 CPU 能帮助他们卖出更多的内存芯片。
转型为 CPU 公司

到 1974 年，Intel 开发了 8 位的 8008，随后很快在 1975 年推出了 8080 处理器。8080 成为 Altair 的核心，而 Altair 正是开启微型计算机革命的产品。不久之后，16 位微处理器 8086 及其降本版本 8088 问世，IBM 选择了 8088 用于其 IBM PC。1985 年，Intel 生产了 32 位的 80386 微处理器，开启了一系列日益强大的微处理器之路，包括 80486、Pentium 以及各种配套的集成电路和采用这些芯片的计算机。PC 的普及使 x86 成为事实上的标准。
到了 386 时代，Intel 决定停止将其 CPU 进行第二来源授权，转而成为唯一供应商。这与时任 CEO Gordon Moore 在面对日本 RAM 制造商的激烈竞争时，决定将重点从存储设备转向 CPU 的举措相呼应。

由于无法获得设计的第二来源授权，其他公司开始克隆这些设计。Intel 通过诉讼将大多数早期克隆公司（如 Chips & Technologies 和 UMC）赶出了市场。在 486 和 Pentium 时代，阻止新贵公司进入市场变得更加困难，但最终这家 Pentium 制造商能够利用专利将除 AMD 之外的所有竞争对手基本清除。是的，Zhaoxin 确实存在并在中国市场销售芯片，但这很大程度上是出于政治原因，而非技术原因。
Intel Inside

Intel 辉煌时期的另一个标志是其营销策略。它将自己定位为高端品牌，告诉你要认准他们的贴纸，并对其他芯片制造商散布疑虑。这很有效。我工作过的一些地方多年来甚至不考虑使用 AMD 处理器，更不用说在 CPU 出现之前的日子里，像 DEC PDP-11 和 VAX 这样的企业级小型计算机中的传统处理器设计，里面装满了由 AMD 制造的分立逻辑芯片和 AMD 2900 系列 ALU。而且在整个 20 世纪 80 年代，AMD 都是 IBM 可靠的第二供应商，不仅提供 CPU，还提供主板上几乎所有其他芯片。
但 AMD 负担不起广告费用，因此他们沦为了杂牌地位，尽管其芯片的兼容性或可靠性绝对没有任何问题。即使是臭名昭著的 Pentium FDIV bug，在 20 世纪 90 年代也几乎没有损害 Intel 作为高端品牌的声誉。

如今，认为购买 AMD 芯片有问题的观念已经减少，这在很大程度上是因为 AMD 在 Athlon 64 一代表现出色，随后又在 Ryzen 一代再次发力，在性能和功耗上与 Intel 保持同步，有时甚至超越他们，因为 Intel 在芯片制造工艺上的领先优势随着时间的推移已经逐渐削弱。仍然有人将其视为高端品牌并出于习惯购买 Intel。但将 Intel 视为唯一选择的日子似乎正在消退，这也反映在公司的股价上。
David Farquhar 是一名计算机安全专业人士、企业家和作家。他从 1991 年开始专业撰写关于计算机的文章，因此当复古计算机还是新事物时，他就在写关于它们的内容了。他从 1994 年开始从事专业的 IT 工作，并自 2013 年起专门从事漏洞管理。他拥有 Security+ 和 CISSP 认证。如今他每周写五次博客，主要关注 1975 年至 2000 年期间的复古计算机和复古游戏。
